title: What Can ZOTHEOS Do For Indigenous People And Nations?
intro: Make knowledge useful. Follow the evidence, identify a decision that matters and prepare a next step you control. Truth, dignity and sovereignty are the standard for judging the work.

This is a practical starting point for people, families, community organizations and Nations worldwide, including people outside government recognition lists. Each community chooses its own priorities and representation. No single story, institution or workflow stands for all Indigenous peoples.

now: Read the public Nations directory, source-linked histories and coverage gaps. Follow Nations’ own websites and official resources.
Use this guide and download its blank action brief. Explore official Theater recordings with their source and viewing notes.
limits: This website does not file applications, represent a Nation, determine citizenship, provide legal or financial advice, negotiate land rights or guarantee an outcome.
The guide has no upload or submission form. It does not collect your planning answers. Linked services have their own privacy rules and requirements.
ZOTHEOS is not yet advised by an Indigenous advisory circle. Inclusion and automated checks are not Nation endorsement or community consent.
The planning steps and future workflows are ZOTHEOS proposals. The cited organizations have not endorsed them.
future: The desktop app remains in internal testing. The Proposed App Workflow blocks below are design proposals to evaluate, not released services or proven outcomes.
Any future assistance needs verified capabilities, appropriate permission, human review and evaluation chosen with the people affected. Your decisions remain yours.

chapters.title: Land, Water And Restoration
chapters.intro: A serious answer to land loss begins with the outcome the affected people want. UNDRIP addresses lands and resources in Article 26, redress including restitution in Article 28, and development priorities and consent in Article 32. These standards matter alongside the particular legal system and the Nation’s own institutions.

steps.title: Begin With The Nation’s Account
steps.text: Use the directory and linked histories to identify the distinct Nation and its own published priorities. Follow the original source. A map, a state label or this directory cannot establish title, a complete homeland boundary or authority to negotiate.

steps.title: Build A Decision Brief
steps.text: For a public proposal affecting land or water, record the project, responsible authority, published documents, verified deadline and the community’s authorized position. Ask which outcome is sought: return of ownership, protection of access, restoration, a decision-making agreement or another remedy. Record these separately; an invitation to advise does not itself transfer ownership.

steps.title: Organize Evidence For Human Review
steps.text: A future, tested ZOTHEOS workflow could compare public project documents, extract dated commitments and draft questions with page references. It would need to preserve uncertainty and original files. Counsel, rights holders and authorized community representatives would assess the evidence and choose the remedy.

verify: Confirm land status, jurisdiction, who can speak for the rights holders and the current procedural rules with qualified local support.
Keep sensitive places and restricted knowledge out of a public brief. A website summary cannot give consent, settle title or predict a court outcome.
chapters.deliverable: A source-linked land-and-water brief with one requested decision, its decision-maker, evidence gaps and a verified next date.
chapters.reflection: Who will hold authority, access and responsibility after the proposed agreement, and who gets to say no?

practice.question: In this hypothetical exercise, how could a public history brief keep work, displacement and land ownership from being treated as the same claim?
steps: Read the Tribe’s linked Land And Timber Industry chapter. Record the publisher’s account of work and displacement, its source title and the period it discusses.
Create separate headings for livelihoods, displacement and ownership. Place only supported statements beneath each; mark a missing record or disputed account as an open question.
If further work is authorized, prepare a list of records to seek and questions for a relevant archive or qualified adviser. Keep private family details and sensitive locations out of a public brief.
practice.boundary: This historical account is not a property-title search, an agreed land claim or evidence of a current remedy. The exercise does not authorize research or negotiation for the Tribe.
practice.reflection: Whose account is missing, and what evidence would be needed before making a stronger claim?

chapters.title: Representation With Decision-Making Power
chapters.intro: Indigenous people can seek influence in national and local institutions while their Nations sustain their own systems of government. UNDRIP Articles 5 and 18 recognize these distinct dimensions. More Indigenous officeholders can be a community goal; meaningful authority, accountability and chosen representation also need attention.

steps.title: Find Practical Voting Resources
steps.text: For US elections, follow NARF’s voter resources for registration, identification, polling access, Native-language assistance and Tribal leaders’ guides. This site connects you to those resources; it does not register voters, endorse a party, recruit candidates or speak for a Nation.

steps.title: Name The Decision And The Seat
steps.text: Separate a public-election goal from a Nation’s own governance process. For the issue you choose, identify the council, school board, agency, legislature or other body with actual authority. Write the decision sought, who is affected and how representatives will report back. Verify current eligibility, deadlines and voting rules through official channels.

steps.title: Compare Public Commitments
steps.text: A proposed ZOTHEOS workflow could place published platforms, meeting records, budgets and later votes beside one another with exact citations. People would set the questions and check context. The system should not infer someone’s identity or political preferences, score a community’s loyalty or make an endorsement in its name.

verify: National representation does not replace a Nation’s own authority or consent. Who represents a Nation is for its own procedures, not ZOTHEOS, to decide.
Check current election and participation requirements. This guide is nonpartisan public information, not campaign or legal representation.
chapters.deliverable: A decision map connecting one issue to the institution that can act, the participation route, a verified date and a public accountability question.
chapters.reflection: Would a person at the table have a meaningful say, resources and accountability to the people affected?

practice.question: Hypothetical reader question: How can I avoid treating different governing bodies as interchangeable when I study a public decision?
steps: Read the Tribe's own government description. In a private note, keep its Legislative/Executive Branch, Judicial Branch and independent Election Commission distinct; record the source URL and the date you read it.

Choose a public decision you are studying. Create a private table with the decision, responsible institution, published rule, date and unanswered questions. Use that institution's own rules rather than transferring the Tribe's structure to another government.
Mark unknown responsibilities as unknown. Separate who makes a decision, who reviews it and who administers an election; keep your notes as a preparation document for qualified human review.
practice.boundary: This is a hypothetical reading and note-making exercise. It does not authorize participation, determine membership or jurisdiction, advise on a legal case, identify a current appeal route, represent the Tribe or establish endorsement. No outreach, filing, submission or transfer of cultural material is part of the exercise.
practice.reflection: Which responsibilities are supported by the institution's own published rules, and which assumptions still need checking?

chapters.title: Recover Records And Keep The Context
chapters.intro: Historical work becomes more useful when another person can trace a statement back to its source. The US National Archives links treaty texts with supporting correspondence, council records and catalog identifiers. Its records are one institutional perspective; a Nation’s own accounts and protocols belong in the research plan.

steps.title: Follow Facts To Their Sources
steps.text: Read a profile’s Facts And Sources and its deeper history links. Notice the difference between an event year and the date the source was checked. The directory’s coverage notes can reveal missing records without turning an omission into proof that a people did not exist.

steps.title: Make An Evidence Ledger
steps.text: For each statement, record the original title, author or institution, date, URL or archive identifier, page, supporting passage and what it does not establish. Keep conflicting accounts side by side. Ask a community archive or historian how to handle names and records before making a family or collective history public.

steps.title: Draft With Verifiable References
steps.text: A possible desktop workflow could help organize a permitted document collection into an evidence table and a timeline. It would need reliable page references and checks for missing or misread text. An extracted sentence is a starting point for review; it cannot decide whether a treaty remains applicable or a legal claim succeeds.

verify: Archives may contain colonial language, omissions and harmful classifications. Explain their context instead of adopting those labels as fact.
Preserve original files and record corrections. Historical rolls, ancestry research and a search result do not determine present-day citizenship or membership.
chapters.deliverable: An evidence ledger that separates sourced statements, interpretations, disputed accounts and unanswered questions.
chapters.reflection: Could someone with a different view inspect the same evidence and see where your conclusion comes from?

practice.question: In this hypothetical exercise, how could someone trace a historical school-aid request without turning a request into proof that aid arrived?
steps: Open the Tribe’s Social Barriers chapter and locate its heading about the 1934 school-aid effort. Record the exact source and the distinction between the historical year and the source-check date.
Start an evidence ledger with separate columns for the request, a response, any decision and any delivery. Leave unsupported columns blank rather than completing the story from an assumption.
Write one bounded archival question, such as which public correspondence records the response. Follow the archive’s access rules and the community’s guidance before sharing family records.
practice.boundary: A reported request does not establish approval, delivery, legal entitlement or the outcome of a separate court case. No private family file is needed to use this exercise.
practice.reflection: Could a reader follow the evidence and see exactly where the account remains incomplete?

chapters.title: Language And Culture Under Community Direction
chapters.intro: A language project can begin with everyday learning and a community’s own goals. FPCC publishes planning, language-nest, family-learning and mentor-apprentice resources. Its FirstVoices tools support community-managed language sites. Availability of a tool or a public recording does not establish permission to copy, translate or train a model on it.

steps.title: Find Community-Led Learning
steps.text: Use Nations’ own links and the FPCC resource guide to locate a suitable starting point. Read who the material is for and what reuse is allowed. This website’s translation guidance concerns public reading text; automated translation is not an authority on an Indigenous language.

steps.title: Plan A Small Learning Project
steps.text: With the relevant speakers and community authority, choose an audience, a modest learning goal and an approved set of materials. Agree on attribution, payment, access, reuse and the ability to withdraw material before recording. Choose an existing community-led resource when it already meets the need.

steps.title: Support A Teacher-Checked Workflow
steps.text: A future ZOTHEOS workflow might organize approved lesson notes or draft practice activities in a language it has been evaluated for. Fluent speakers would check every output. It must not invent translations. Any use of a person’s voice or reuse of recordings would need separate permission, applicable rights checks and speaker review.

verify: Ask which materials may be public, shared within a community or kept restricted. Do not infer a common rule across Nations.
Keep speaker expertise central and compensate work appropriately. A fluent-sounding model output may still be wrong.
chapters.deliverable: A community-approved learning plan describing the audience, permitted materials, speaker review and access rules.
chapters.reflection: Will this project strengthen speakers and learners while leaving the community in control of its knowledge?

practice.question: In this hypothetical exercise, how could I prepare a reading plan that follows a community's own learning resources without claiming to teach or translate its language?
steps: Open the Tribe's own Learning Tools page. Record the publisher, source URL, the date you read it and any stated audience or access conditions.
Make a short bookmark list of public resources you want to understand. Keep the original links and labels; do not copy lessons, recordings or word lists into a new public collection.

Write the questions that a qualified speaker or teacher would need to resolve before a learning activity could be shared. Mark pronunciation, local usage and reuse permissions as unverified until appropriately checked.
practice.boundary: This is a private reading-plan exercise, not a language lesson, translation, teaching qualification, invitation or permission to reuse cultural material. Public availability does not authorize voice imitation or model training. No outreach, submission or recording is part of this exercise.
practice.reflection: What can I learn by following the original resource, and what still requires a speaker's knowledge and the community's permission?

chapters.title: Control Over Data And Digital Work
chapters.intro: The CARE principles connect Indigenous data governance with collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics. FNIGC describes ownership, control, access and possession through the First Nations principles of OCAP®. FNIGC is explicit that these are specifically principles of First Nations in Canada; each Nation’s own protocols remain essential.

steps.title: Read The Governance Frameworks
steps.text: Use the cited CARE paper and FNIGC’s own explanation before selecting a tool. These are external learning resources. ZOTHEOS has not been certified against them or endorsed by their authors. OCAP® is a registered trademark of the First Nations Information Governance Centre (FNIGC).

steps.title: Write The Rules Before Gathering Data
steps.text: Decide who authorizes collection, who benefits, who can see or change records, where copies sit, how retention works and who can stop use. Separate public research from citizenship files, health records, restricted knowledge and precise sensitive locations. Write down permitted uses and a contact route for correction or withdrawal.

steps.title: Test A Community-Controlled Workspace
steps.text: A proposed local workflow could help organize permitted material under access and retention rules that the community chooses. It would require verified security, export, deletion and network behavior. Local storage alone does not establish consent, collective control, confidentiality or protection from a compromised device.

verify: Assess the actual system, contracts and data flows before adding sensitive material. A product description is not a security audit.
This guide has no upload or submission form. Keep the downloaded planning brief in a location you choose; do not put private records into it for publication.
chapters.deliverable: A data-use agreement checklist with decision authority, purpose, access, retention, permitted reuse and an exit plan.
chapters.reflection: Can the people whose knowledge or records are involved understand the use, change the rules and stop it?

chapters.title: Children, Families And Community Connections
chapters.intro: NICWA explains the Indian Child Welfare Act as a US law with defined requirements for covered child-custody proceedings. Its application involves specific criteria; it is not a universal rule for every family or country. A useful guide helps someone reach the right specialist while protecting the child’s privacy.

steps.title: Reach The Original Guidance
steps.text: Open NICWA’s explanation and family resources from its own site. This page provides a reading route, not case intake or an eligibility finding. A documentary can give historical context, but cannot establish what should happen in an individual proceeding.

steps.title: Prepare For A Qualified Conversation
steps.text: If a US child-welfare matter may involve ICWA, speak promptly with the child’s Tribe and a qualified attorney or legal service, as NICWA advises. Privately organize notices, dates, questions and existing case contacts. Ask how the relevant law, Tribal membership determination and current court process apply; avoid posting identifying records publicly.

steps.title: Keep Any Draft Assistance Narrow
steps.text: A possible ZOTHEOS workflow could help a person organize questions from documents they are authorized to use. It would require rigorous privacy and accuracy checks. It must not decide membership, legal eligibility, custody, placement or the best interests of a child, and it must not delay professional help.

verify: Current deadlines and court instructions require qualified case-specific advice. Check local law; do not export US ICWA assumptions to another jurisdiction.
A family’s dignity includes control over its story. Obtain appropriate authority before sharing any record or account involving a child.
chapters.deliverable: A private question list and document index for a qualified adviser, with verified dates and identifying information kept out of public material.
chapters.reflection: Does the next step protect the child’s safety, relationships, privacy and the community’s lawful role?

chapters.title: Resources For Community-Chosen Futures
chapters.intro: The Native CDFI Network describes work to strengthen Native community development financial institutions and access to capital. It includes Native American, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian communities in its mission. A resource connection can help someone explore options; it is not evidence of eligibility, an open funding round or an affordable loan.

steps.title: Find A Relevant Starting Point
steps.text: Follow the Network’s current resources and the Nation’s own published economic or education programs. Read the actual provider’s terms and service area. ZOTHEOS does not lend, award grants, verify a program’s current availability or receive financial applications.

steps.title: Prepare A Realistic Project Brief
steps.text: Define a project chosen by the people involved: a business, language program, food initiative, community facility or another need. List the budget, skills, ongoing costs, intended beneficiaries and decision authority. Compare the provider’s current criteria, obligations, fees and repayment conditions with qualified advice where appropriate.

steps.title: Help Prepare Draft Materials
steps.text: A proposed workflow could turn an approved budget and project notes into a draft narrative, a missing-information list and a source-linked comparison of published opportunities. People would verify every figure and representation. No invented impact metrics, financial promises or automatic applications belong in the output.

verify: Confirm all eligibility, cost, repayment, ownership and deadline details with the actual provider. This guide is not financial advice.
Ask who owns the result and carries the risk. A project should build community capacity rather than transfer control through unclear terms.
chapters.deliverable: A project brief with a checked budget, responsibilities, ongoing costs, provider questions and an honest list of missing information.
chapters.reflection: Will the benefits, skills and decision-making stay with the people the project is meant to serve?

practice.question: Hypothetical reader question: How could I prepare a dated checklist for a small gathering that I am responsible for?
steps: Read the two dated Nation posts. In a private note, label one account as a plan and the other as a reported start; keep the source dates beside the links.
For a gathering you control, list your own venue permission, facilities, equipment and weather checks. Write who on your own team will check each item and by when.
Make a one-page preparation checklist with a review date and an unresolved-items column. Recheck your own arrangements before deciding whether the gathering can proceed.
practice.boundary: This is a hypothetical exercise in the reader's own planning. The Nation's old notices do not authorize access to its land, attendance, volunteering, fundraising or use of cultural material, and they do not establish present project status. No outreach or submission is part of this example.
practice.reflection: Which parts of my note are dated source facts, and which decisions and responsibilities belong to my own project?

chapters.title: Education That Keeps Evidence And Dignity Together
chapters.intro: The public website already offers cited Nation profiles, source-linked reading and a Theater of official viewing destinations. Those are starting points for learning. Their existence does not mean every statement in a film has been independently verified or that any Nation has endorsed ZOTHEOS.

steps.title: Read Beyond A Film
steps.text: Choose a profile and read its own sources alongside a relevant Theater recording. Keep the viewing type, content notes, historical period and access limits in view. Look for living community work and continuity as well as accounts of harm.

steps.title: Create A Responsible Learning Session
steps.text: Define a question and audience, choose permitted materials, and provide context and a way to step away from difficult content. Separate the source’s statement from your interpretation. Include community-authored material and correct mistakes openly. Seek the appropriate permission before using voices, artwork or cultural material in a public project.

steps.title: Draft A Source-Checked Learning Pack
steps.text: A future workflow could help prepare a reading sequence, glossary or discussion questions from material permitted for that purpose. A qualified educator and relevant community reviewers would check it. It should preserve disagreement and uncertainty rather than manufacture consensus or a single pan-Indigenous account.

verify: A public link is not a licence to rehost a film, imitate a voice or copy restricted knowledge. Check the publisher and community conditions.
Sources have limits and can change. When an account is disputed, attribute it and show what evidence remains unresolved.
chapters.deliverable: A learning plan with one question, direct source links, viewing notes, an explanation of uncertainty and a correction route.
chapters.reflection: Will the audience leave better able to check a claim and recognize the people behind it?

practice.question: In this hypothetical exercise, how could I correct a learning note I control so it identifies this Nation accurately and links to its own account?
steps: Read the Nation's introduction and the Southeastern Mvskoke Nation section of its history. Record the preferred name, the source URL and the date you read it.

Revise a note you control to name the Southeastern Mvskoke Nation specifically. Attribute the 1981 organization date to its history, and keep that government date separate from the much longer history of its people.
Add direct links to the Nation's own introduction and history. Mark any relationship to another Creek government that you have not verified as an open question; save the revision for your own review.
practice.boundary: This is a reader-controlled learning exercise. A shared language, Creek history or similar name does not establish a single government, citizenship, authority to represent the Nation or permission to reuse cultural material.
practice.reflection: Which assumption changed when I separated the history of a people from the organization and name of a particular government?

chapters.title: Worldwide Rights, Local Routes
chapters.intro: UNDRIP offers a worldwide rights framework, including cross-border relationships in Article 36. Practical routes vary by place. The UN’s legal commentary discusses its influence and relationships with other law; a declaration, a domestic statute, a treaty and a court judgment should not be treated as interchangeable.

steps.title: Start With The Right People And Place
steps.text: Use worldwide directory navigation to find the distinct people, Nation or representative organization. Then read its own sources. Country and region labels help browsing; they do not define identity, exclusive homelands or who may speak for a community.

steps.title: Find The Applicable Process
steps.text: Identify the decision, the relevant jurisdiction and the community-authorized institution or adviser. Ask which domestic, regional, treaty or international process is actually available, with what requirements and risks. A general rights statement does not by itself establish an enforceable remedy, an admissible complaint or a guaranteed response.

steps.title: Compare Without Flattening Differences
steps.text: A proposed ZOTHEOS workflow could compare public accounts across borders while retaining original language, dates and separate legal contexts. It would need reviewed translations and local expertise. It should not turn another Nation’s agreement, legal status or practice into a universal template.

verify: Confirm the current rules and the authority of any representative or intermediary. This page does not submit complaints or conduct outreach.
Check translation and local terminology with people qualified to interpret them. Recognition categories do not exhaust the world’s Indigenous identities.
chapters.deliverable: A jurisdiction-and-process map with the community’s chosen objective, applicable sources, adviser questions and a verified next step.
chapters.reflection: What needs to change in this place, and whose knowledge and authority are needed to decide how?

chapters.title: Make Repair Specific And Accountable
chapters.intro: A practical proposal for repair should say what changes, who decides, who pays and how the affected people judge the result. The planning method below is a ZOTHEOS proposal for organizing work. It is not an agreement by a Nation, a legal remedy or evidence that any promised benefit has happened.

steps.title: Use The Brief And Show The Gaps
steps.text: Download the plain-text action brief from this page. Choose one chapter and fill the blank fields in a place you control. The directory’s coverage report and corrections route can help you identify missing public information. This page does not collect your answers.

steps.title: Ask For A Concrete Commitment
steps.text: For a proposal you are authorized to advance, name the requested change, responsible institution, resources, consent process, milestone and correction route. Examples to evaluate include a community-directed language budget, a documented access commitment or an agreed land-restoration process. Keep compensation, ownership, representation and service delivery distinct; the affected rights holders decide what is acceptable.

steps.title: Track Promises Against Evidence
steps.text: A future workflow could compare a public commitment with dated records of what followed. People would choose the measures and decide whether publication is appropriate. A polished report, a meeting or a positive sentiment score must not be substituted for a demonstrated change in authority, access or conditions.

verify: Agree on what would count as progress and what would trigger revision or stopping. Record actual observations and uncertainty; do not invent participation, consent or outcomes.
For allies and institutions: ask what support is wanted, resource the work fairly and accept refusal. The guide is not a mandate to initiate a project in someone else’s name.
chapters.deliverable: A community-directed commitment record: requested change, authorized decision-maker, resources, evidence, review date and a way to correct or stop.
chapters.reflection: If the people affected said this did not help, could the project change course and return control?

practice.question: Hypothetical reader question: How could I distinguish a completed land transaction from later plans and check what a public restoration announcement actually establishes?
steps: Read the Yurok Tribe's July 28, 2026 land-transfer announcement. Start a private ledger with separate columns for the statement, the event date, the publication date, the evidence and what remains unknown. Record the June 30 conveyance separately from the August 1 opening date announced in the release.

Separate ownership, operation, restoration work, public access and future construction into different rows. Label each row as a reported completed action, an announced plan or a question needing evidence. A future cultural-center plan is not a completed building; a scheduled opening is not a record of later access.

For a public commitment you are studying, name one observable change and the public record that could demonstrate it. Preserve the original statement and date, then add any later source as a new entry. If no later record has been checked, write that limitation instead of marking success or failure.

Finish a one-page commitment ledger with the responsible institution, evidence gaps and your next review date. Use it to prepare a precise question for qualified human review; keep sensitive places and private community information out of the public note.
practice.boundary: This is a reading and evidence-organizing exercise, not a property-title search, a legal finding, an audit of the Tribe or permission to visit, collect material or act for the rights holders. The release is the Tribe's public account; it does not establish that every planned benefit later occurred or that another land claim would have the same route or outcome.
practice.reflection: What changed in ownership or authority, what was only promised, and what evidence would the people affected need to judge whether repair was useful?
